title: There is no objective view of Earth
subtitle: Tilting our world perspective
author: Elleke Boehmer
introduction: The famous image of Earth from space looks neutral—but it was quietly turned to put the north on top. Professor Elleke Boehmer argues that this small adjustment captures a much larger habit of mind, and that there is no objective perspective by which to view the world. By reading literature from the far southern hemisphere, we can flip our planetary perspective, loosen the grip of northern dominance, and learn to see the world as a more connected, fragile whole.
body:
The “blue marble” photograph of Earth taken in 1972 from Apollo 17 is one of the most famous photographs of the twentieth century. At first glance, it is as neutral an image of our planetary home as we can imagine—the green and blue orb floating in dark space. This is why it has served as an emblem for a variety of environmental movements, a neat image of our place in the universe, the only one we have.

But now, let us look more closely. Most reproductions show the globe with the North Pole “at the top,” with white cloud curdling up over Africa below. From its very first appearance, however, the photograph was inverted to conform to global conventions. In fact, Apollo 17’s camera had first pictured the planet as bearing the vast, white cap of Antarctica.

Reading forms an especially potent resource for moving away from embedded philosophical standpoints, and, in this case, opens windows to look at the earth from other angles, including from the south.

From then on, the reangling of the earthly blue marble has perfectly illustrated something important about how we look at the world. The general view is fixated on developments in the northern hemisphere. Events occurring across the great continental sweep that extends from Eurasia into North America are deemed to be more important than anything happening elsewhere. Globalization has been dominated by these regions. At the end of 2025, many media summaries of the first quarter of the twenty-first century featured not a single global event from south of the equator, not even a volcanic explosion or a tsunami, the southern disasters that sometimes make the news. Only around 11% of the world’s population lives in the southern hemisphere. Most of it is ocean. For decades, newspapers and media outlets have confidently assumed that nothing much of significance will happen in these regions.

But what if we decide not to revert to the northern default? My book Southern Imaginingexplores this question.

It reflects on the phenomenological difficulty of our ever seeing the world from an objective standpoint, limited as we are by our geopolitical perspective and our plain human subjectivity. But, if we allow for these constraints, we may also be able to map pathways towards an alternative point of view, one that will allow us to counterbalance and mutually assess different subjective standpoints, especially, in this case, on the planet. Such calibrated views may emerge from our discovering more about so-called marginalized cultures and their alternative frameworks of knowledge, and also by learning other languages. Reading forms an especially potent resource for moving away from embedded philosophical standpoints, and, in this case, opens windows to look at the earth from other angles, including from the south.

It is true that southern views, in particular, are not easy to get at. How do we approach cultures and geographies that have not been included in Western symbolic systems? Whereas the East was conventionally seen and studied as a perfumed Other, the far south, the lands facing the hostile Southern Ocean, including the great southern polar icecap itself, have for centuries been taken as altogether more unknown, strange and frightening. On Earth, the cold southern edges of the world are the closest correlate we have for the very distant. Edgar Allan Poe, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Mary Shelley, Jules Verne, and many more have all pictured the far south as the outer limit of the world, a place of radical change and horror.

Meanwhile, southerners, including writers and artists, often see themselves as far away from where things count, internalising the wider global sense of their relative insignificance.

Southern Imagining pulls our centre of gravity into the far southern hemisphere by placing readers imaginatively and critically in Australia, southern Africa, South America, the Southern Ocean, and the extended Pacific. The book takes travelogues, log books, journals, poems, and fictions to explore ways of looking at our planet that disrupt the dominant northern view. By reading writers ranging from the Portuguese epic poet Luís de Camões through Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Charles Darwin, and Katherine Mansfield, to Jorge Luis Borges, Alexis Wright, and Tara June Winch, it helps us to reverse our habitual planetary perspective and rearrange our sensory geography.

SUGGESTED READING The strange allure of borders By Emily Thomas

In The Voyage of the Beagle (1839), for instance, we see Charles Darwin looking into the depths of time that the geologically layered cliffs of Patagonia reveal to him, while also noticing the commonalities that connected natural worlds and human cultures from around the southern hemisphere. Piecing together these assembled observations as he circumnavigated the planet, he came gradually to notice similar patterns of evolutionary change that manifested across the southern continents, far-flung though they were. Some years before he touched down on the Galapagos Islands, he had started to develop his ideas about natural selection, in effect by taking the expansive canvas of the far south as his drafting board. For Darwin, southern distances were transformative not merely because of their remoteness but because they nonetheless demonstrated interrelationship.

Closer to the present day, the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges and the South African-born, now Australian novelist J. M. Coetzee, though they both write in respectful dialogue with European literary traditions from countries like Ireland, France and Russia, embed in their writing a certain obsession with places outside time, or fuera del tiempo, as Borges puts it. The seemingly infinite regression of space and light of the Pampas, in the case of Borges, or of the Karoo for Coetzee, brings into their writing a differently angled, more volumetric understanding of the wider planet, and a greater sense of interconnection across it. Borges, in a story like ‘El Sur’ or ‘The South’ from Ficciones (1953), speaks of waking up to heightened feelings of relationality, in part from reading tales of other cultures, like the Arabian Nights, in part from his perspective writing in Buenos Aires, on the South American littoral. Coetzee remarks in 2017 on the “instant” recognizability of far southern spaces to all southerners, no matter where in the hemisphere’s temperate zones they find themselves. Shared austral awareness produces a sense of collocation, of living and thinking parabolically or side-by-side with others in the wider south, no matter how faraway they may be.

Borges and Coetzee, like Darwin, and like a host of other writers, take observation and writing itself as media through which to establish, even if intermittently and fleetingly, a far southern perspective, a different kind of magnetoreception. Through engaging with their work, northern readers as well as southern discover a new orientation. It is as if they are located in the south, at least for the duration of their reading or listening. For southern readers, the situation is different again. Reading legends, songs and poems about and, especially, from the south they feel that they are no longer so far away from the centres that count. They are at last in place.

The south-tilted world map**,**re-centred through song and story, can allow us to claim a more involved sense of belonging to our planet.

The perspective shift south may be effortful but the rewards of the changed view are many. To begin, we learn to see the world more holistically, as Darwin did. We discover the north as a counterpart to the south, as well as vice versa. We develop the imaginative means of working at very different scales at once, and of shuttling between them. We find that the seemingly very faraway may have impacts upon the smallest and most personal aspects of our lives. We may even find ways of acting on this perception.

For decades if not centuries, the far south of the world was treated as a bottomless rubbish tip, a vast sink for our waste products, including CO2. The Australian interior and Pacific islands were taken as sites for nuclear testing, as if the dire effects on local people and environments did not matter. The southern Indian Ocean is used to this day as a dump for Starlink debris.

Now, that forgetting is coming back to haunt us. The ignored Southern Ocean has, across the past thirty years, been warming faster than any other ocean in the world. Scientists did not till quite recently much notice or measure this acceleration, because it was distant, seemingly outside the places that counted. The oversight potentially holds grave consequences for the rest of the planet. Quite apart from the effects of this temperature change on the integrity of the Western Antarctic ice sheet, the Ocean’s powerful cold currents regulate oceanic pulses from the Northern Atlantic to the South Pacific. Ultimately, these currents determine weather patterns everywhere.

We are invited to practice southern thinking by flipping the script on the northern view of the world. The south-tilted world map**,**re-centred through song and story, can allow us to claim a more involved sense of belonging to our planet. We can offer a changed global map that brings remote regions to mind as if they were close by. As the oceans heat up and the ice caps melt, this alternative view is becoming ever more pressing for all of us to share. South-centered thinking upturns and recharges the way we see ourselves and our planet.
